Does robotic inguinal hernia repair improve pain, complications, recurrence, return to normal activity, or quality of life compared with conventional laparoscopic repair? Assess randomized evidence, operative time, and costs

Decision support — the clinician decides.

AT A GLANCE
No consistent patient benefit; costs more.
- Cost: $3258 robotic vs $1421 laparoscopic [1]
Main caveat: Small trials with short follow-up.

BOTTOM LINE
No consistent patient benefit; longer and costlier [1].
Certainty: Low — small, heterogeneous trials

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR CLINICAL PRACTICE
Default choice: Laparoscopic repair.
Who may benefit: Not shown.
Counselling: Recovery is similar.
Cost per case: not known in India; $3258 vs $1421 in RIVAL

CONFLICTING EVIDENCE
- Learning curve: operative time in rTAPP falls significantly after about 32 cases. Pooled early-versus-late operative time gap is 17 (not traced) min. Trial operative-time penalties may therefore reflect early learning curve, not steady-state.
- A high-volume robotic surgeon past the learning curve reports a median incision-to-closure time of 38 min, same-day discharge, low pain and no recurrences. Suggests operative time and recovery can match or beat laparoscopy at the steady state.
- Uncontrolled UK learning-curve series supports the safety of a structured EHS training pathway. Median rTAPP time was 56 min unilateral and 101 min bilateral. Complications were 3.3% and there were 2 recurrences at 6 months.
- A technique report asserts a theoretical robotic advantage in complex hernias. It is opinion and a single case, with no outcome data.
- Narrative review states the evidence for MIS in bilateral and recurrent hernias is limited. This supports the gap in the evidence base rather than refuting the conclusion.
- A 2026 narrative review is consistent with the researcher's conclusion.
- Operative time is NOT consistently longer with robotic repair. The RCTs conflict: DIRECT (40632168) and ROLAIS (40277023) found robotic faster, while RIVAL, ROGER and VOLTAIRE found it longer. The MA pooled difference is non-significant with I2 about 98% (42927985). The learning curve (about 32 cases, 17 (not traced) min, 42747553) and surgeon experience probably drive this. Say 'variable, often longer', not 'longer'.
- Not every RCT found 'no benefit'. ROLAIS (40277023, n=139 (not traced)) reported fewer complications, less inflammation and more same-day discharge with robotic repair, but it is open-label and single-centre. VOLTAIRE (40450465) found more patients back to normal activity at 14 d (39% vs 5%), but it is small (n=59), a secondary outcome and unblinded. The honest summary is 'no consistent patient benefit across trials, with two trials showing early signals'.
- Cost is the most robust finding against robotic repair (RIVAL $3258 vs $1421, and several observational and model studies). The cost data come mostly from observational or modelled studies plus one RCT. Costs depend on the platform and the institution and are not RCT-grade. The 2026 RCT MA reported no significant cost difference on low or very-low certainty evidence (42625069), so state that the cost direction is consistent but the certainty is low.
- Long-term outcomes (chronic pain, recurrence, quality of life) are essentially unproven. The only RCT long-term data are RIVAL at 1-2 years with about 25% loss to follow-up (35578051). Absence of evidence of benefit does not equal evidence of no benefit. Recurrence differences in observational meta-analyses (42541618 (not traced), RR 0.32) are low certainty and confounded.
- Complex, recurrent, bilateral, obese and inguinoscrotal hernias: no RCT has addressed these subgroups. The conclusion applies to mostly primary, unilateral hernias in selected, experienced-surgeon settings. Robotic advantages there are plausible but untested (prospective SCAR study is only a protocol, 42040509 (not traced)).
- Evidence base is low or very-low certainty and heterogeneous: small trials, mostly rTAPP vs lTAPP (only ROGER used lTEP as comparator), mostly high-income expert centres, an Indian RCT (42527734) null, and an open-console platform in VOLTAIRE. Findings may not generalise to other platforms (Hugo, Dexter, Versius) or to trainee surgeons.
- Surgeon-side benefits are the most consistent robotic signal (ergonomics in VOLTAIRE and a 2026 ergonomics MA 42842114 (not traced), lower NASA-TLX workload in ROGER) but they are not patient outcomes. Surgeon-side benefits should be reported separately from the patient-outcome verdict.
- No HerniaSurge or EHS guideline statement on robotic versus laparoscopic inguinal repair was found in PubMed. Do not claim a guideline position. The only society item is an EHS training pathway (40842882), which is not a recommendation to prefer either approach.

GUIDELINES AND CONSENSUS STATEMENTS
- European Hernia Society: mesh repair for adults — “Mesh repair is recommended for all adults with an inguinal hernia.” [2]

APPLICABILITY
Case mix: primary unilateral
India and cost: not known
Training: a reasonable index case

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THIS ANSWER
- a large multicentre RCT with long follow-up

- DIRECT reports surgeon experience inconsistently [1].

CONFLICTING EVIDENCE
- Learning curve: operative time in rTAPP falls significantly after about 32 cases. Pooled early-versus-late operative time gap is 17 (not traced) min. Trial operative-time penalties may therefore reflect early learning curve, not steady-state.

- Uncontrolled UK learning-curve series supports the safety of a structured EHS training pathway. Median rTAPP time was 56 min unilateral and 101 min bilateral. Complications were 3.3% and there were 2 recurrences at 6 months.
- A technique report asserts a theoretical robotic advantage in complex hernias. It is opinion and a single case, with no outcome data.
- Narrative review states the evidence for MIS in bilateral and recurrent hernias is limited. This supports the gap in the evidence base rather than refuting the conclusion.
- A 2026 narrative review is consistent with the researcher's conclusion.
- Operative time is NOT consistently longer with robotic repair. The RCTs conflict: DIRECT (40632168) and ROLAIS (40277023) found robotic faster, while RIVAL, ROGER and VOLTAIRE found it longer. The MA pooled difference is non-significant with I2 about 98% (42927985). The learning curve (about 32 cases, 17 (not traced) min, 42747553) and surgeon experience probably drive this. - Not every RCT found 'no benefit'. ROLAIS (40277023, n=139 (not traced)) reported fewer complications, less inflammation and more same-day discharge with robotic repair, but it is open-label and single-centre. VOLTAIRE (40450465) found more patients back to normal activity at 14 d (39% vs 5%), but it is small (n=59), a secondary outcome and unblinded. The honest summary is 'no consistent patient benefit across trials, with two trials showing early signals'.
- Cost is the most robust finding against robotic repair (RIVAL $3258 vs $1421, and several observational and model studies). The cost data come mostly from observational or modelled studies plus one RCT. Costs depend on the platform and the institution and are not RCT-grade.
